Our new customer acquisition is going up, retention is holding but wallet share of our retained customers is going down. What could explain this? 
Qualitative in-sighting bridges the gap between your dashboards and your customer's behaviour. It shouldn’t be a one time exercise for milestones like brand/product/market extension, but an ongoing way for founders to keep their ears to the ground and understanding how shifting category, environment and competitive dynamics are impacting their consumers and their messy realities. Read on to find out how xto10x has discovered and used insights from qualitative studies to shape marketing and product roadmaps for agile startups.

Neeraj Aggarwal
4w

A founder’s day begins and ends with dashboards - hundreds of metrics at their fingertips, covering every possible data point in the product and consumer funnel. And justifiably so - data is tangible, granular, dissectable, and real-time. 

But therein lies a trap -  basing business decisions on the trendlines of AOVs, CACs and repeat rates, without engaging with the messy, non-linear and quite often irrational behaviour of the very human consumers behind those numbers.

Data tells you what is happening. Consumer insights help explain why.

Companies tend to sacrifice qualitative research at the altar of speed, cost and efficiency, all of which are real constraints in a hyper-competitive and agile reality. Yet every number on that dashboard is a consumer decision waiting to be interpreted. Behind a repeat rate sits the question - did this earn a place in my life week after week; CAC  - did this feel like it was for someone like me; AOV - what is this worth to me. 

Qualitative research is a uniquely rich way of understanding this underlying behaviour and logic. It can be one of the strongest tools in your arsenal - a continuous interpreter of your own data and the category at large, enabling a meaningful evolution of your brand’s journey.

The carousel below shows what good qualitative research can reveal - and how those insights can change who you target, what you build and which problems you solve.

"CM1 is under pressure. We need to cut ops costs." Right diagnosis. Wrong prescription.

The companies that have moved CM1 by 5 to 7 points haven't just lowered costs. Their sales loss reduced. Their gross-to-net improved. What looks like a cost story is actually a revenue story, a conversion story, and a retention story wearing an ops label.

Most ops teams are optimising OTIF. But, the metric that moves CM1 the most is D1/D2 promise and delivery: roughly 2 points on its own. It doesn't show up in your logistics cost line as much as it shows up in your RTO rate, your conversion at checkout, and your retention.

80% of the cost opportunity is outside your warehouse. In a 3PL rate card that hasn't been renegotiated since your volumes doubled. In an RTO % that no one owns. In packaging weight no one has benchmarked. And in the fulfilment model, SKU portfolio and structural cost leakage in your marketplace channel. Your team is optimising the 20% they can see.

Just three capabilities needed to solve this dichotomy (an ops design team, a 3PL vendor management function, a structured S&OP process) costing one to two people each. You will see results from month three onwards.

Swipe to see the levers, the benchmarks, and what the P&L looks like when ops is working the way it should.

Great leadership talent is rare. A well-designed compensation model is among the most critical levers that meaningfully improves your odds of hiring great leaders, and retaining them.

Only 30% of leaders in the ecosystem score high on our assessment of readiness to lead at scale. You are competing hard for a very thin slice of an already small talent pool. 

And the stakes are high. Only 1 in 50 startups break out to $25M+ in revenue, and those that do take about ten years to get there. We studied a set of companies that had P90+ leadership talent from the start...every one of them broke out, and got there faster.

Compensation is also already your biggest cost line item. People costs are typically ~60-65% of revenue of a growth-stage startup, and the leadership layer is the most expensive part of that number, and almost always the least well-designed.

This is where most founders lose a crucial lever. One template doesnt do justice, because you are not paying one kind of leader. You are typically paying for four different personas, and they value different things:

The Builder: the smart generalist. "I am here for the mission. Please ensure my wealth creation if we do well."
The Professional: the functional specialist. "Pay me what the market pays. I have done this before."
The Owner: the P&L leader. "Give me the P&L, and a share of what I create with it."
The Practitioner: the craft leader. "Don't make me manage people to get paid like a leader."

"Faster delivery always costs more." This is perhaps the most misplaced assumption in operations.

Around 80% of your supply chain speed is locked in the moment you decide your network architecture. How many warehouses you run, where they are, and what flows between them sets your performance floor. Everything your operations team does after that is just working inside a ceiling someone else set.

In most scaling startups, that ceiling was set by accident, taking leases where a landlord said yes or where a 3PL provider had spare capacity.

When you treat speed as a structural network design exercise rather than an operational grind, you stop making the classic trade-off. You don't just deliver faster, but your cost per order falls, RTO and Cancellations drop, EDD breaches stay in control and platform conversion improves.

Read to see how a leading e-commerce platform moved D2 from 20% of orders to more than 80%, significantly improving their overall P&L.

Every founder obsessively seeks a path to growth. What’s surprising is how few realize their 'core customers' are already writing the playbook for them. 

Let's call this core base “power users” and the rest light users.

We have seen that power users, who seldom account for more than 10-12% of the total users acquired, make up for the majority of the contribution margin in most consumer businesses.

And yet most founders spend huge amounts of resources solving for every customer. Averages blunt clarity and lead to expensive mistakes.

“Our CSAT is 4.7 on 5. Yet our repeat rate hasn't moved in three quarters”.

This comes up in almost every consumer business we meet. Scores look healthy. However, consumer behavior doesn't match. Time to look deeper at Relationship NPS, a metric that tracks trust, advocacy, and long-term value, not just one-off satisfaction.

What is Relationship NPS (RNPS)?
Transactional CSAT measures satisfaction with a single interaction. RNPS measures the strength of the overall relationship. Is the customer truly invested in your brand?

Why brands need RNPS:
1. 2.5x lifetime value: RNPS Promoters spend more than twice as much as customers who simply gave a good CSAT score.
2. 3x referral power: Promoters don't just mention you, they champion you. That's 3x more effective than transactional CSAT promoters.
3. Retention armor: These customers forgive slip-ups because they're bought into YOU, not just a transaction.
4. Similar brands, different outcomes: Two players in the same category can post near-identical CSAT scores. Yet one was compounding repeating customers while the other had to keep refilling the funnel through new users. RNPS explained the gap.

Where most NPS strategies go wrong:
1. The loudest complaint gets fixed first. But loud isn't the same as important, so ₹50L gets spent and the score barely moves.
2. One score for everyone. Why a first-time buyer never returns is rarely why a regular customer drifts away. Average them and the number describes nobody.
3. A metric nobody owns. No name against the top problems, no target, no date to check again.

How to leverage RNPS for growth:
1. Ask at the right time: post-milestones, not just post-transaction.
2. Find what truly matters: identify the key drivers shaping the whole experience, not one touchpoint. This isn't new science, but it used to mean an agency, three weeks, and ₹10-15L a wave. Now it runs on your own survey data in minutes with AI.
3. Know your strengths and weaknesses: measure CSAT on your most critical NPS drivers, like fit and comfort for innerwear, or selection variety for quick-commerce etc

Bottom line: businesses thrive when relationships beat transactions. Do you measure what truly matters?

Most startups think they have an S&OP process. What they actually have is a monthly review meeting.

A well-run S&OP process can unlock 10 to 15% additional revenue by reducing avoidable sales loss. For a ₹100 crore consumer brand, that's ₹80L to ₹1cr of incremental revenue every month, plus ₹1 to 2cr freed up in working capital from better inventory decisions.

Yet very few companies get it right. Not because they don't care, but because the process itself is broken. Five mistakes we see most often:

1.⁠ ⁠S&OP typically reports into Demand or Supply, which is a mistake. S&OP should be an independent orchestrator reporting to the CFO.
2.⁠ ⁠Most S&OP meetings become postmortems discussing what happened last month instead of preventing what's about to happen next month.
3.⁠ ⁠Analysis happens inside the meeting with senior leaders debating SKU level issues which should have been pre-analysed.
4.⁠ ⁠Every SKU gets equal attention. Your hero and long-tail SKUs shouldn't be planned with the same rigor.
5.⁠ ⁠Inventory decisions are reactive. Stock gets shifted between channels, solving today's problem while creating tomorrow's.

The good news? AI has changed what's easily possible now. It can monitor the plan in real time, flag at-risk SKUs, run the analysis teams never have time for, and highlight where intervention is needed before revenue is lost.

The best S&OP meetings don't explain the past. They answer three questions:

Where is next month's revenue at risk?
What should we do this week?
How much can still be recovered if we act now?

The real opportunity isn't using AI to make planning faster. It's using AI to make planning better. For the first time a 10/10 S&OP process can be run without spending days.

We’re hiring interns at xto10x @ Growth Practice.

To get a flavour of the role, let me share what the last 5 months here have been like for me.

When I joined the team, I never anticipated the diversity of the problem statements I’d be working with.

My first project was helping improve the sales funnel % for a Series B startup. At the same time, I was also working with another company on their launch in Malaysian market. Two completely different industries. Two very different problems. But both tied to one thing of moving their top-line revenue in a meaningful way.

The context switching was intense. But what really stood out was the depth we go into for every problem. You can’t stay at the surface. Very quickly, I realised that if you’re not clear about what exactly you’re solving for, you’ll get lost trying to solve everything.

That’s been my biggest learning so far. It is to investigate problems with clarity & defining the real question before jumping to solutions. In growth, it’s easy to optimise something. It’s much harder to ensure you’re optimising the right thing.

I’ve also started appreciating the shift between thinking like an operator and thinking like a strategist. Top-down clarity but grounded in messy on-ground startup realities and i’m still learning. But being this close to founders and real revenue decisions accelerates your thinking in ways that are hard to replicate elsewhere.

The internship we’re opening up is what I’d call a “deep generalist” role in our Growth practice. You’ll work across industries, problem statements, and functions always anchored around unlocking revenue for startups.

It’s about ownership & learning how startups actually scale.

I’ve shared a detailed PDF about the role.
Application link is in the comments.

Last date to apply is 4th March. Excited to see who joins us next!
